question: Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets and define $f:A\times B\to B\times A$ by $f(a,b)=(b,a)$. Prove that $f$ is both one-one and onto.
explanation:
Verification of one-one property
Let $(a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2)\in A\times B$ and suppose $$f(a_1,b_1)=f(a_2,b_2)$$ By the definition of $f$, $$(b_1,a_1)=(b_2,a_2)$$ Equality of ordered pairs gives $$b_1=b_2\quad\text{and}\quad a_1=a_2$$ Hence, $$(a_1,b_1)=(a_2,b_2)$$ Therefore, equal images arise only from equal elements of the domain, and $f$ is one-one.

Verification of onto property
Let $(b,a)$ be an arbitrary element of $B\times A$. Since $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, the ordered pair $(a,b)$ belongs to $A\times B$. By the definition of $f$, $$f(a,b)=(b,a)$$ Thus, every element of $B\times A$ is the image of an element of $A\times B$. Therefore, $f$ is onto.

Final Result
The function $f:A\times B\to B\times A$ defined by $f(a,b)=(b,a)$ is both one-one and onto.

options.A: $f$ is one-one but not onto because some ordered pairs in $B\times A$ have no pre-image.
options.B: $f$ is onto but not one-one because two different ordered pairs can produce the same reversed pair.
options.C: $f$ is neither one-one nor onto unless $A=B$.
options.D: $f$ is both one-one and onto because equality of the reversed pairs implies equality of the original pairs, and every $(b,a)\in B\times A$ has the pre-image $(a,b)\in A\times B$.
